summary: Defines an Extensible Provisioning Protocol extension called Registry Maintenance Notification. Through it, registry servers can notify registrars about maintenance events and registrars can query the servers about them. This helps registrars plan around planned downtime or changes.

plainLanguage.summary: A shop posts a sign saying when it will be closed for fixing, and you can ask it at any time.

questions: how can registrars find out about registry downtime
what is the epp maintenance extension
subtitle: How registry servers notify registrars about scheduled maintenance events.

tldr.problem: Registries regularly maintain and upgrade their systems, causing temporary service interruptions. Currently, each registry informs registrars about maintenance in different formats, making it difficult for registrars managing many registries to coordinate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9167 defines an EPP extension that lets registry servers send standardized maintenance notifications to registrars. Registrars can query for upcoming maintenance events or receive notifications when events change.
tldr.outcome: A standardized approach across registries simplifies registrar planning and reduces the need for manual communication about downtime windows.

today: RFC 9167 remains a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines how modern EPP-based registries notify registrars about maintenance events using standardized XML messages delivered through EPP commands and poll responses.

sections.title: The Problem of Maintenance Notifications
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), defined in RFC 5730, is the standard protocol used for domain name registration between registries and registrars. Registries regularly update their systems to improve service quality, implement new services, or upgrade to newer standards. These updates may temporarily make services unavailable.

Currently, registries notify registrars about maintenance events in different, non-standardized ways. With the growth of the DNS namespace and new registries, registrars now manage many separate relationships with different registries. Each registry using its own notification format creates coordination headaches. RFC 9167 solves this by standardizing how maintenance notifications flow through EPP itself.
sections.plainLanguage: When a shop needs to close for repairs, it tells its customers different ways depending on the shop. This RFC makes all shops use the same messaging system to tell registrars when they are closed.

sections.title: How Maintenance Events Are Described
sections.content:
A maintenance event has several pieces of information. The registry assigns a unique identifier to each event. The maintenance can affect multiple systems (EPP, WHOIS, DNS, Portal, RDAP) with different impact levels: full outage, partial outage, or no impact. Each event also specifies which environment is affected (production, testing, staging, development, or custom), when it starts and ends, and whether it is planned or emergency maintenance.

The registry can describe which top-level domains are affected. Registrars can also query whether they need to take action—for example, whether clients will need to reconnect or whether registrar code changes are required.
sections.plainLanguage: When maintenance is scheduled, the registry says what is broken, how bad it is, which store sections are affected, when it starts and stops, and what customers need to do about it.

sections.title: Querying and Receiving Maintenance Information
sections.content:
EPP provides two main ways to access maintenance information. The <info> command lets registrars ask for details about specific maintenance events or request a list of all current and upcoming events. The registry responds with the event details in a standardized XML structure.

Alternatively, registries can use EPP's <poll> mechanism to push notifications to registrars. When a maintenance event is created, updated, completed, or deleted, the registry sends a poll message. Registrars acknowledge these messages to dequeue them, ensuring they receive each notification. The RFC defines five poll types: create for new events, update for changes, delete for cancellations, courtesy for reminders, and end to signal completion.
sections.plainLanguage: Registrars can either ask the registry "what maintenance is happening?" and get a list, or the registry can automatically send messages saying "maintenance happening now" and wait for the registrar to acknowledge them.

sections.title: The Data Structure
sections.content:
The RFC defines an XML schema for the maintenance extension. Each maintenance item is an element with child elements for the unique ID, type of maintenance, affected systems, environment type, start and end times in UTC, reason (planned or emergency), optional detail URL, optional description, affected top-level domains, and whether client intervention is needed.

Dates and times must be in RFC 3339 format with UTC timezone. Internationalized domain names must use A-label form (the ASCII-compatible encoding). The extension namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:maintenance-1.0, allowing multiple versions of the extension to coexist as registries transition.
sections.plainLanguage: The information is stored in XML with fields for what is happening, when, which parts of the system, and whether you need to do anything about it. Dates are written in a standard format so every system understands them.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
RFC 9167 inherits the security model from RFC 5730, which defines EPP security. A critical requirement is that servers must only provide maintenance information to authorized clients. If a registrar queries for a maintenance event it is not authorized to see, the server returns an authorization error or reports the event does not exist. Similarly, the list of affected TLDs returned in a response must be filtered to show only TLDs the registrar manages.

Authorization decisions happen at the time the poll message is created, not when the registrar retrieves it. This prevents authorized registrars from later losing access to information they were entitled to at the time of dispatch.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry must check that a registrar is allowed to know about maintenance affecting its own domains. A registrar cannot see maintenance events for domains it does not manage.

sections.title: The Status of This Extension
sections.content: RFC 9167 is a Proposed Standard from December 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines version 1.0 of the EPP maintenance extension. The RFC expects that future versions may emerge; servers should support multiple versions in parallel during transitions to allow registrars to upgrade at their own pace.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the current standard way for registries to tell registrars about maintenance. New versions may come later, but this one is how it works today.
